claim: Ciliary and rhabdomeric photoreceptor cells represent two main lines of photoreceptor-cell evolution in animals.
source: Ciliary and rhabdomeric photoreceptor cells represent two main lines of photoreceptor-cell evolution in animals.
evidence: This is a statement about photoreceptor cell evolution that is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: Ciliary photoreceptors are presynaptic to the rhabdomeric circuit in Platynereis larvae.
source: We used connectomics to map synaptic paths between ciliary and rhabdomeric photoreceptors in the planktonic larva of the annelid Platynereis and found that ciliary photoreceptors are presynaptic to the rhabdomeric circuit.
evidence: This claim is supported by connectomics data from serial-section transmission electron microscopy showing synaptic connections.

claim: The ciliary photoreceptors are UV-sensitive in Platynereis larvae.
source: The ciliary photoreceptors are UV-sensitive and mediate downward swimming in non-directional UV light, a behavior absent in ciliary-opsin knockout larvae.
evidence: This is supported by absorption spectrum data showing c-opsin1 absorbs UV light and behavioral assays showing UV-specific responses.

claim: UV avoidance overrides positive phototaxis mediated by the rhabdomeric eyes in Platynereis larvae.
source: UV avoidance overrides positive phototaxis mediated by the rhabdomeric eyes such that vertical swimming direction is determined by the ratio of blue/UV light.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral experiments showing that UV light causes downward swimming even when larvae initially swim upward toward the light source.

claim: The ratio of blue/UV light increases with depth in seawater.
source: Since this ratio increases with depth, Platynereis larvae may use it as a depth gauge during vertical migration.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about light attenuation in seawater and field data from the Mediterranean mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: Platynereis larvae may use the blue/UV light ratio as a depth gauge during vertical migration.
source: Since this ratio increases with depth, Platynereis larvae may use it as a depth gauge during vertical migration.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the observed behavioral responses to different light ratios and the known properties of light attenuation in seawater.

claim: Rhabdomeric PRCs have apical microvillar specializations (rhabdom) that store the opsin photopigments.
source: Rhabdomeric PRCs have apical microvillar specializations (rhabdom) that store the opsin photopigments.
evidence: This is established knowledge about rhabdomeric photoreceptor cell morphology, supported by citations.

claim: The visual photoreceptor cells in most protostome eyes are rhabdomeric and express rhabdomeric (r-) opsins.
source: The visual photoreceptor cells in most protostome eyes, including the compound eyes of arthropods, the pigment-cup eyes of annelids and the camera or stalk eyes of mollusks, are rhabdomeric and express rhadomeric (r-) opsins (Arendt et al., 2002; Cowman et al., 1986; Katagiri et al., 2001; Katagiri et al., 1995; Ovchinnikov et al., 1988; Pollock and Benzer, 1988; Randel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research on protostome photoreceptor cells.

claim: The visual eyes of vertebrates have ciliary PRCs (rods and cones) where the ciliary (c-) opsin photopigment is stored in specialized ciliary membrane compartments.
source: In contrast, the visual eyes of vertebrates have cPRCs (rods and cones) where the ciliary (c-) opsin photopigment is stored in specialized ciliary membrane compartments (Jan and Revel, 1974; Nir et al., 1984).
evidence: This is established knowledge about vertebrate photoreceptor cells, supported by citations.

claim: The class of opsin expressed in a PRC generally correlates with the cell's morphological type.
source: The class of opsin expressed in a PRC generally correlates with the cell's morphological type, with cPRCs usually expressing c-opsins and rPRCs expressing r-opsins (Arendt, 2003; Arendt et al., 2004; Randel et al., 2013; Vopalensky et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on photoreceptor cell types and opsin expression.

claim: Both photoreceptor cell types likely coexisted in the last common ancestor of bilaterians.
source: Given their broad phylogenetic distribution and shared opsin expression, both photoreceptor cell types likely coexisted in the last common ancestor of bilaterians.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic distribution of the two photoreceptor cell types across bilaterian animals.

claim: In Platynereis, non-pigmented brain cPRCs with ramified cilia express a ciliary type opsin (c-opsin1).
source: In Platynereis, non-pigmented brain cPRCs with ramified cilia express a ciliary type opsin (c-opsin1) (Arendt et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research on Platynereis photoreceptor cells.

claim: The pigmented larval eyespots and the adult eyes mediate early- and late-stage larval phototaxis, respectively, in Platynereis.
source: The pigmented larval eyespots and the adult eyes mediate early- and late-stage larval phototaxis, respectively (Gühmann et al., 2015; Jékely et al., 2008; Randel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on Platynereis phototaxis.

claim: Trochophore larvae have a pair of pigmented eyespots with a rPRC that directly innervates the adjacent ciliary band.
source: Trochophore larvae (approximately 1–2.5 days post fertilization) have a pair of pigmented eyespots with a rPRC that directly innervates the adjacent ciliary band.
evidence: This is supported by previous research on Platynereis larval anatomy and circuitry, as indicated by citations in the manuscript.

claim: The eyespot rPRC is cholinergic and expresses r-opsin3 in Platynereis trochophore larvae.
source: This rPRC is cholinergic and expresses r-opsin3 (Jékely et al., 2008; Randel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on Platynereis photoreceptor cells.

claim: Nectochaete larvae develop two pairs of adult eyes with several rPRCs coexpressing r-opsin1, r-opsin3 and Go-opsin.
source: Nectochaete larvae (approximately 3–5 days post fertilization) develop two pairs of adult eyes with several rPRCs coexpressing r-opsin1, r-opsin3 and Go-opsin (Gühmann et al., 2015; Randel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on Platynereis photoreceptor cells.

claim: C-opsin1 was recently shown to absorb UV light.
source: C-opsin1 was recently shown to absorb UV light.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent research on c-opsin1 spectral properties.

claim: The c-opsin1-expressing cPRCs mediate circadian entrainment by ambient UV light.
source: This suggests that the c-opsin1-expressing cPRCs mediate circadian entrainment by ambient UV light (Tsukamoto et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a suggestion based on a citation to previous research, indicating it is an inference from that work.

claim: The RGW interneurons synapse on the Schnörkel premotor interneurons (INsn).
source: First, the RGW interneurons synapse on the Schnörkel premotor interneurons (INsn)(Figure 1E–G and Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by connectomics data from serial-section transmission electron microscopy and shown in figures.

claim: Six interneurons (INpreMN) are postsynaptic to the RGW interneurons and presynaptic to the ventral motoneurons (vMNs) of the visual circuit.
source: Second, we identified six interneurons (INpreMN) that are postsynaptic to the RGW interneurons and presynaptic to the ventral motoneurons (vMNs) of the visual circuit (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is supported by connectomics data from serial-section transmission electron microscopy and shown in figures.

claim: Two putative mechanosensory neurons (MS1 and MS2) are postsynaptic to the RGW cells and presynaptic to the vMNs and INpro interneurons of the visual circuit.
source: Third, two putative mechanosensory neurons bearing a sensory cilium and a collar of microvilli and located in the median head (MS1 and MS2)(Bezares-Calderon et al., 2018) are postsynaptic to the RGW cells and presynaptic to the vMNs and INpro interneurons of the visual circuit (Figure 1E–G and Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by connectomics data from serial-section transmission electron microscopy and shown in figures.

claim: The cPRC circuit feeds hierarchically into the visual rPRC circuit.
source: Thus, the cPRC circuit feeds hierarchically into the visual rPRC circuit (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is an inference based on the connectomics data showing synaptic connections from cPRC to rPRC circuits but not vice versa.

claim: The cPRCs could influence phototaxis, a behavior mediated by the rhabdomeric eyes and eyespots.
source: This suggests that the cPRCs could influence phototaxis, a behavior mediated by the rhabdomeric eyes and eyespots (Gühmann et al., 2015; Jékely et al., 2008; Randel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the synaptic connectivity data and previous knowledge about phototaxis.

claim: Each cPRC has 12–15 basal bodies each with a root and an extensively branched sensory cilium.
source: Each cPRC has 12–15 basal bodies each with a root and an extensively branched sensory cilium.
evidence: This is supported by serial-section transmission electron microscopy data.

claim: The total sensory membrane surface area of a cPRC is approximately 276 μm2.
source: Based on the average diameter and total length of all branches in one cPRC we estimated a membrane area of 276 μm2
evidence: This is calculated from measurements obtained from serial-section transmission electron microscopy data.

claim: The sensory membrane surface area of a Platynereis cPRC is approximately 10 times smaller than the total disk membrane surface area of rat rods.
source: which is approximately 10 times smaller than the total disk membrane surface area of rat rods (Mayhew and Astle, 1997).
evidence: This is a comparison based on the measured membrane area of Platynereis cPRCs and cited data on rat rods.

claim: Platynereis cPRCs are sensitive enough to mediate acute light sensation.
source: This suggests that Platynereis cPRCs are sensitive enough to mediate acute light sensation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the calculated membrane surface area of the cPRCs.

claim: Purified Platynereis c-opsin1 reconstituted with 11-cis-retinal absorbed in the UV range with a λ-max of 384 nm in the dark spectrum.
source: The reconstituted pigment absorbed in the UV range with a λ-max of 384 nm in the dark spectrum and a λ-max of 370 nm in the dark-light difference spectrum (Figure 2E)
evidence: This is supported by in vitro absorption spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Purified Platynereis c-opsin1 reconstituted with 11-cis-retinal had a λ-max of 370 nm in the dark-light difference spectrum.
source: The reconstituted pigment absorbed in the UV range with a λ-max of 384 nm in the dark spectrum and a λ-max of 370 nm in the dark-light difference spectrum (Figure 2E)
evidence: This is supported by in vitro absorption spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The cPRCs have a high resting calcium level when imaged with a low-intensity 488 nm laser.
source: When imaged with a low-intensity 488 nm laser, the cPRCs had a high resting calcium level and the GCaMP6s signal highlighted their sensory cilia.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data using GCaMP6s.

claim: When cPRC cilia are locally stimulated with 405 nm light, the calcium level drops transiently at the cPRC somata and then increases strongly.
source: When the cPRC cilia were locally stimulated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) for 5 min with 405 nm light (140–250 times more photons on the sensory cilia than by the imaging laser), the calcium level dropped transiently at the cPRC somata and then increased strongly.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in figures.

claim: 405 nm stimulation of cPRCs indicates transient cPRC hyperpolarization followed by depolarization.
source: This indicates transient cPRC hyperpolarization followed by depolarization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed calcium dynamics in response to 405 nm stimulation.

claim: When cPRCs are stimulated with a 488 nm laser of equal photon flux to 405 nm, they show prolonged hyperpolarization only, without depolarization.
source: However, when the cPRCs were stimulated with a 488 nm laser of equal photon flux, they showed prolonged hyperpolarization only, without depolarization (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: When 405 nm stimulation is switched off during the hyperpolarization phase, the cPRCs still depolarize afterwards.
source: When the 405 nm stimulation was switched off during the hyperpolarization phase (after 20 s), the cPRCs still depolarized afterwards (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Four neurons corresponding to the four RGW interneurons follow the activity pattern of the cPRCs upon 405 nm stimulation.
source: 405 nm stimulation of the cPRCs also changed the activity of other neurons in the larval brain. Four neurons followed the activity pattern of the cPRCs (Figure 2J; Figure 2—figure supplement 2). These cells correspond by position to the four RGW interneurons, which together with the four NOS interneurons are direct postsynaptic targets of the cPRCs (Figure 1G)(Williams et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data and connectomics data showing these cells are postsynaptic to cPRCs.

claim: Two flask-shaped sensory neurons (SNearly) in the middle of the anterior nervous system depolarize upon 405 nm stimulus onset.
source: Additionally, two flask-shaped sensory neurons (SNearly) in the middle of the anterior nervous system depolarized upon stimulus onset.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: Two sensory cells (SNlate) flanking the SNearly cells depolarize later, in parallel with the rising phase of cPRC activity.
source: Two further sensory cells (SNlate) flanking the SNearly cells depolarized later, in parallel with the rising phase of cPRC activity (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The RGW interneurons and the SNearly sensory neurons only respond to 405 nm stimulation but not to 488 nm stimulation.
source: The RGW interneurons and the SNearly sensory neurons only responded to 405 nm stimulation (with opposite sign) but not to 488 nm stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data comparing responses to different wavelengths.

claim: The SNlate neurons in some larvae also respond to 488 nm stimulation but these responses are weaker than to 405 nm.
source: The SNlate neurons in some larvae also responded to 488 nm stimulation but these responses were weaker (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The cPRCs and their postsynaptic neurons respond differentially to violet and blue stimulation.
source: Thus, the cPRCs and their postsynaptic neurons respond differentially to violet and blue stimulation, with only violet light inducing cPRC depolarization and consistent changes in the activity of postsynaptic neurons.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the calcium imaging data showing different responses to 405 nm and 488 nm light.

claim: When Platynereis larvae are stimulated with non-directional UV light, they start to swim downward.
source: When the larvae were stimulated with non-directional UV light, they started to swim downward.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays in a vertical column setup.

claim: Platynereis larvae swim down to UV-violet light (between 340–420 nm) but not to longer wavelengths (>420 nm).
source: The larvae swam down to UV-violet light (between 340–420 nm) but not to longer wavelengths (>420 nm, Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays with monochromatic light of different wavelengths, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The action spectrum of UV-avoidance closely matches the absorption spectrum of c-opsin1.
source: The observations that UV-avoidance can be triggered by non-directional light and has an action spectrum that closely matches the absorption spectrum of c-opsin1 (Figure 2E) suggest that the response is mediated by the non-pigmented cPRCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the behavioral action spectrum with the c-opsin1 absorption spectrum.

claim: UV-avoidance in Platynereis is likely mediated by the non-pigmented cPRCs.
source: The observations that UV-avoidance can be triggered by non-directional light and has an action spectrum that closely matches the absorption spectrum of c-opsin1 (Figure 2E) suggest that the response is mediated by the non-pigmented cPRCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the action spectrum match and the non-directional nature of the response.

claim: Phototaxis is present in Platynereis larvae at 27 hpf.
source: Phototaxis, but not UV-avoidance was already present at 27 hpf, at a stage when the larval eyespots are already functional (Jékely et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays at different developmental stages and citations to previous work.

claim: UV avoidance appears in Platynereis larvae at 36 hpf.
source: UV avoidance appeared at 36 hpf, approximately coinciding with the morphological differentiation of cPRCs (after 32 hpf, as judged by the appearance of the ramified cilia)(Figure 3C)
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays at different developmental stages shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The appearance of UV avoidance at 36 hpf approximately coincides with the morphological differentiation of cPRCs.
source: UV avoidance appeared at 36 hpf, approximately coinciding with the morphological differentiation of cPRCs (after 32 hpf, as judged by the appearance of the ramified cilia)(Figure 3C)
evidence: This is a correlation observed between behavioral onset and morphological development.

claim: UV avoidance appears long before the differentiation of the adult eyes in Platynereis larvae.
source: but long before the differentiation of the adult eyes (at 72 hpf)(Fischer et al., 2010; Jékely et al., 2008; Randel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by developmental timing data and citations to previous work.

claim: Platynereis larvae show UV-violet-light avoidance that is independent of phototaxis.
source: Thus, Platynereis larvae show UV-violet-light avoidance that is independent of phototaxis, can be induced by non-directional stimulus light, and is likely mediated by the UV-violet-responding non-pigmented cPRCs.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the behavioral and developmental data.

claim: When stimulated with 380 nm light from above, both early- and late-stage Platynereis larvae first swim upward towards the light and then swim downward.
source: When we used 380 nm stimulus light, both early- (41 hpf) and late-stage (3 and 4.5 dpf) larvae first swam upward towards the light (for approximately one minute), and then swam downward (Figure 3D, Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays shown in Figure 3D and Video 2.

claim: The upward-swimming phase in response to 380 nm light from above is phototaxis.
source: These results indicate that the upward-swimming phase is phototaxis, which is then overwritten by the UV-avoidance response.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral observations and the fact that the upward phase is not observed with non-directional light.

claim: In response to illumination with 340–400 nm light from above, Platynereis larvae swim downward after prolonged stimulation.
source: In response to illumination with 340–400 nm light, larvae swam downward after prolonged stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays with different wavelengths of directional light.

claim: In response to illumination with 440–540 nm light (early-stage) or 440–600 nm light (late-stage) from above, Platynereis larvae swim upward.
source: In response to illumination with 440–540 nm light (early-stage) or 440–600 nm light (late-stage), larvae swam upward (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays shown in Figure 3E.

claim: 420 nm light does not trigger vertical displacement of Platynereis larvae.
source: 420 nm light did not trigger the vertical displacement of the larvae.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays with different wavelengths.

claim: The swimming direction of Platynereis larvae can be switched several times by changing the wavelength of light from 380 nm to 520 nm.
source: The swimming direction could be switched several times by changing the wavelength of the light from 380 nm to 520 nm (Figure 3F)
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The behavioral switch in swimming direction does not habituate even after sustained exposure to light.
source: demonstrating that this behavioral switch does not habituate even after sustained exposure to light.
evidence: This is an inference based on the repeated switching behavior observed in the experiments.

claim: Directional UV-violet light first triggers upward-swimming phototaxis which is then overridden by the downward-swimming UV-avoidance response.
source: These results indicate that directional UV-violet light first triggers upward-swimming phototaxis (the pigmented eyes are sensitive in the UV-violet range [Jékely et al., 2008; Gühmann et al., 2015]), which is then overridden by the downward-swimming UV-avoidance response likely mediated by the cPRCs.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the behavioral data and previous knowledge about eye sensitivity.

claim: Directional blue/cyan light only triggers phototaxis in Platynereis larvae.
source: Directional blue/cyan light only triggers phototaxis.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays with different wavelengths.

claim: The switching in behavioral response cannot be explained as a wavelength-dependent alternation between positive and negative phototaxis.
source: Importantly, the switching in behavioral response cannot be explained as a wavelength-dependent alternation between positive and negative phototaxis, since early-stage larvae are exclusively positively phototactic (Jékely et al., 2008)(until 72 hpf [Randel et al., 2014]), yet already show the behavioral switch in swimming direction (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral data and previous knowledge about larval phototaxis.

claim: At high 380/480 nm photon ratios, Platynereis larvae swim downward.
source: At high 380/480 ratios, larvae swam downward, while at low ratios larvae swam upward.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays with mixed wavelength light shown in Figure 3G.

claim: At low 380/480 nm photon ratios, Platynereis larvae swim upward.
source: At high 380/480 ratios, larvae swam downward, while at low ratios larvae swam upward.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays with mixed wavelength light shown in Figure 3G.

claim: At a 40% 380/480 nm photon ratio, Platynereis larvae remain at a constant average depth despite being exposed to directional light stimulus.
source: At a 40% 380/480 ratio, larvae remained at a constant average depth (Figure 3G), despite being exposed to a directional light stimulus.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Mixing UV light with 660 nm red light does not induce upward swimming at any 380/660 ratio.
source: Mixing the same intensity UV light as before with 660 nm red light (a wavelength to which larvae do not respond phototactically at the intensity used (Figure 3E)) did not induce upward swimming at any 380/660 ratio (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays shown in Figure 3G.

claim: A reduction in UV intensity alone does not cause a switch in swimming direction in Platynereis larvae.
source: This experiment shows that a reduction in UV intensity alone does not cause a switch in swimming direction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of 380/480 and 380/660 ratio experiments.

claim: UV avoidance and phototaxis act antagonistically and cancel each other out under certain wavelength ratios, resulting in no net vertical swimming.
source: These results suggest that UV avoidance and phototaxis act antagonistically and cancel each other out under certain wavelength ratios, resulting in no net vertical swimming.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral data with mixed wavelength light.

claim: The antagonistic interaction of UV avoidance and phototaxis is consistent with the presence of a ratio-chromatic depth gauge in Platynereis larvae.
source: This is consistent with the presence of a ratio-chromatic depth gauge in Platynereis larvae.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral data and the known properties of light attenuation in seawater.

claim: The c-opsin1 knockout line was generated by TALEN-mediated genome editing with an 8 bp deletion in the third exon.
source: To test whether c-opsin1 mediates the UV-violet response in Platynereis larvae, we used a c-opsin1 Platynereis knockout line generated by TALEN-mediated genome editing. The TALENs targeted the third exon of c-opsin1 and induced an 8 bp deletion (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used to generate the knockout line.

claim: In homozygous c-opsin1Δ8/Δ8 larvae, the cPRCs have low resting calcium level.
source: In homozygous c-opsin1Δ8/Δ8 larvae, the cPRCs had low resting calcium level and neither hyperpolarized nor depolarized upon 405 nm stimulation (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: In homozygous c-opsin1Δ8/Δ8 larvae, the cPRCs neither hyperpolarize nor depolarize upon 405 nm stimulation.
source: In homozygous c-opsin1Δ8/Δ8 larvae, the cPRCs had low resting calcium level and neither hyperpolarized nor depolarized upon 405 nm stimulation (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: c-opsin1 in Platynereis cPRCs is required for an elevated resting calcium level in the dark state.
source: Thus, c-opsin1 in the Platynereis cPRCs is required for an elevated resting calcium level in the dark state and for hyperpolarization and subsequent depolarization upon 405 nm exposure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of wild-type and c-opsin1 knockout larvae.

claim: c-opsin1 in Platynereis cPRCs is required for hyperpolarization and subsequent depolarization upon 405 nm exposure.
source: Thus, c-opsin1 in the Platynereis cPRCs is required for an elevated resting calcium level in the dark state and for hyperpolarization and subsequent depolarization upon 405 nm exposure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of wild-type and c-opsin1 knockout larvae.

claim: The high resting calcium level in the cPRCs indicates a dark current.
source: The high resting calcium level in the cPRCs indicates a dark current, a characteristic of vertebrate rods and cones (Hagins et al., 1970).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed high resting calcium level and knowledge about vertebrate photoreceptors.

claim: Homozygous c-opsin1Δ8/Δ8 larvae swim upward (positive phototaxis) in response to 480 nm light, similar to wild type larvae.
source: Similar to wild type larvae, homozygous c-opsin1Δ8/Δ8 larvae swim upward (positive phototaxis) in response to 480 nm light.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays comparing wild-type and mutant larvae.

claim: Homozygous c-opsin1Δ8/Δ8 larvae have a defective UV-avoidance response.
source: However, c-opsin1Δ8/Δ8 larvae have a defective UV-avoidance response.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays comparing wild-type and mutant larvae.

claim: Wild type Platynereis larvae swim downward after an initial upward-swimming phase in response to UV light, whereas c-opsin1Δ8/Δ8 larvae continue to swim upward.
source: Whereas wild type larvae swim downward after an initial upward-swimming phase, c-opsin1Δ8/Δ8 larvae continue to swim upward, showing sustained positive phototaxis in response to UV light (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays shown in Figure 4D.

claim: An additional, c-opsin1-independent UV-avoidance mechanism may exist in Platynereis larvae.
source: The magnitude of upward swimming diminishes, with close to 0 vertical displacement between 1.5–2 min after UV onset. This indicates that an additional, c-opsin1-independent UV-avoidance mechanism may exist in Platynereis larvae
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation that c-opsin1 mutants show reduced but not completely absent UV avoidance.

claim: c-opsin1 is a critical mediator of UV-avoidance in Platynereis larvae.
source: These results show that c-opsin1 is a critical mediator of UV-avoidance.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the behavioral defects observed in c-opsin1 knockout larvae.

claim: The loss of c-opsin1 is expected to disrupt the depth gauge in Platynereis larvae.
source: The loss of c-opsin1 is expected to disrupt the depth gauge since in c-opsin1 mutants both cyan and UV light induce sustained positive phototactic behavior which is likely mediated by the pigmented eyes with a broad spectral sensitivity (380–540 nm [Jékely et al., 2008]).
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral phenotype of c-opsin1 mutants and the proposed depth gauge mechanism.

claim: The depth gauge in Platynereis larvae is formed by the antagonistic interaction of two distinct behaviors mediated by two distinct types of photoreceptor systems with different spectral sensitivities.
source: Our results are consistent with the presence of a ratio-chromatic depth-gauge in the planktonic larvae of Platynereis dumerilii. The depth gauge is formed by the antagonistic interaction of two distinct behaviors, mediated by two distinct types of photoreceptor systems with different spectral sensitivities.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the behavioral and physiological data presented.

claim: The rPRCs mediate phototaxis to a broad range of wavelengths between UV and green light in Platynereis larvae.
source: The rPRCs mediate phototaxis to a broad range of wavelengths between UV and green light, while the cPRCs mediate UV-violet avoidance.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays and previous research on rPRC spectral sensitivity.

claim: The cPRCs mediate UV-violet avoidance in Platynereis larvae.
source: The rPRCs mediate phototaxis to a broad range of wavelengths between UV and green light, while the cPRCs mediate UV-violet avoidance.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays, calcium imaging, and knockout experiments.

claim: Under UV-violet light, after approximately 30 s the UV-violet avoidance response overrides an initial phototactic response in Platynereis larvae.
source: Under UV-violet light, after approximately 30 s the UV-violet avoidance response overrides an initial phototactic response.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays showing the time course of responses to UV light.

claim: At a set UV/blue ratio, the two opposing behaviors (UV avoidance and phototaxis) cancel each other out in Platynereis larvae.
source: At a set UV/blue ratio, the two opposing behaviors cancel each other out.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays with mixed wavelength light.

claim: Due to the differential attenuation of UV and blue light in seawater, the UV/blue ratio mechanism could allow Platynereis larvae to stay at a certain depth in the ocean.
source: Due to the differential attenuation of UV and blue light in seawater, this mechanism could allow the larvae to stay at a certain depth in the ocean.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the behavioral data and known properties of light attenuation in seawater.

claim: The cPRCs express a UV-absorbing opsin in Platynereis larvae.
source: The cPRCs express a UV-absorbing opsin, have a high resting calcium level and react by hyperpolarization and subsequent depolarization to violet light (405 nm).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro absorption spectroscopy data.

claim: The cPRCs have a high resting calcium level in Platynereis larvae.
source: The cPRCs express a UV-absorbing opsin, have a high resting calcium level and react by hyperpolarization and subsequent depolarization to violet light (405 nm).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: The cPRCs react by hyperpolarization and subsequent depolarization to violet light (405 nm) in Platynereis larvae.
source: The cPRCs express a UV-absorbing opsin, have a high resting calcium level and react by hyperpolarization and subsequent depolarization to violet light (405 nm).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: The cPRCs mediate an UV-violet avoidance response characterized by downward swimming in Platynereis larvae.
source: The cPRCs mediate an UV-violet avoidance response characterized by downward swimming.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays and knockout experiments.

claim: The action spectrum of UV-violet avoidance behavior matches the absorption spectrum of c-opsin1 in Platynereis larvae.
source: The action spectrum of this behavior matches the absorption spectrum of c-opsin1 and the response is severely impaired in c-opsin1 knockouts, demonstrating a critical role for c-opsin1 in mediating it.
evidence: This is supported by comparing behavioral action spectra with in vitro absorption spectra.

claim: The UV-violet avoidance response is severely impaired in c-opsin1 knockouts, demonstrating a critical role for c-opsin1 in mediating it.
source: The action spectrum of this behavior matches the absorption spectrum of c-opsin1 and the response is severely impaired in c-opsin1 knockouts, demonstrating a critical role for c-opsin1 in mediating it.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays with c-opsin1 knockout larvae.

claim: The depolarizing response in the cPRCs shows a similar delayed onset as UV-violet avoidance, suggesting that the behavior is due to cPRC depolarization.
source: The depolarizing response in the cPRCs shows a similar delayed onset as UV-violet avoidance, suggesting that the behavior is due to cPRC depolarization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal correlation between cPRC depolarization and behavioral response.

claim: cPRC depolarization occurs even if the stimulus light is switched off during the hyperpolarizing phase.
source: Intriguingly, the depolarization also occurs if the stimulus light is switched off during the hyperpolarizing phase.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: cPRC depolarization is not due to direct opsin activation but to a sustained cell-autonomous or non-autonomous signal.
source: This implies that cPRC depolarization is not due to direct opsin activation but to a sustained cell-autonomous or non-autonomous signal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that depolarization occurs even after the light is switched off.

claim: The high calcium level in the cPRCs suggests the possibility of the tonic release of a neurotransmitter (probably acetylcholine) in the dark.
source: The high calcium level in the cPRCs suggests the possibility of the tonic release of a neurotransmitter (probably acetylcholine) in the dark, similar to the tonic release of glutamate by vertebrate photoreceptors (Heidelberger et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the high resting calcium level and comparison with vertebrate photoreceptors.

claim: Blue illumination (488 nm) induces cPRC hyperpolarization but no subsequent depolarization.
source: Blue illumination (488 nm) also induces cPRC hyperpolarization, but no subsequent depolarization.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: The cPRC hyperpolarization response to blue light may be mediated by another opsin expressed in the cPRCs.
source: This response may be mediated by another opsin expressed in the cPRCs.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed response to blue light.

claim: c-opsin2 with a maximal absorption at 490 nm is a candidate opsin for mediating the blue light response in cPRCs.
source: One candidate is c-opsin2 with a maximal absorption at 490 nm (Ayers et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion based on the spectral properties of c-opsin2 and a citation.

claim: cPRC hyperpolarization induced by violet or blue light has different downstream consequences.
source: One surprising observation is that cPRC hyperpolarization induced by violet or blue light has different downstream consequences.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data showing different responses in postsynaptic neurons.

claim: The different downstream consequences of violet vs. blue light may be due to the engagement of different signaling cascades by the different opsins.
source: This may be due to the engagement of different signaling cascades by the different opsins.
evidence: This is a speculative inference to explain the observed differences in downstream responses.

claim: The cPRC circuit connects to the Ser-h1 serotonergic ciliomotor neurons.
source: The cPRC circuit connects to the Ser-h1 serotonergic ciliomotor neurons (Verasztó et al., 2017), suggesting that the modulation of ciliary activity may contribute to UV avoidance.
evidence: This is supported by connectomics data and a citation.

claim: The modulation of ciliary activity may contribute to UV avoidance in Platynereis larvae.
source: The cPRC circuit connects to the Ser-h1 serotonergic ciliomotor neurons (Verasztó et al., 2017), suggesting that the modulation of ciliary activity may contribute to UV avoidance.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the synaptic connectivity.

claim: The cPRCs and their direct postsynaptic targets are part of the neurosecretory brain center of the Platynereis larva.
source: The cPRCs and their direct postsynaptic targets are part of the neurosecretory brain center of the larva (Williams et al., 2017a)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Knocking out one neuroendocrine signaling component leads to strong defects in UV avoidance in Platynereis larvae.
source: and knocking out one neuroendocrine signaling component leads to strong defects in UV avoidance (unpublished results).
evidence: This is mentioned as unpublished data, suggesting experimental evidence exists but is not shown.

claim: The cPRC circuit connects to the circuit of the rhabdomeric eyes via the cholinergic RGW interneurons.
source: We found that the cPRC circuit connects to the circuit of the rhabdomeric eyes via the cholinergic RGW interneurons and their distinct downstream synaptic pathways.
evidence: This is supported by connectomics data.

claim: The RGW neurons provide inputs to the phototactic circuit at the level of the INsn, INpro and the vMN cells.
source: The RGW neurons provide inputs to the phototactic circuit at the level of the INsn, INpro and the vMN cells.
evidence: This is supported by connectomics data.

claim: The strongest and most direct connection between the cPRC and rPRC circuits is through synapses from the RGW cells to the INsn neurons.
source: The strongest and most direct connection between the cPRC and rPRC circuits is through synapses from the RGW cells to the INsn neurons.
evidence: This is supported by connectomics data showing synapse counts.

claim: Cholinergic input from the RGW cells to the INsn premotor interneurons may antagonize phototaxis.
source: Cholinergic input from the RGW cells to these premotor interneurons may antagonize phototaxis.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the synaptic connectivity.

claim: The two photoreceptor cell types may have evolved antagonistic functions early in evolution.
source: Our findings suggest that the two types may have evolved antagonistic functions early in evolution.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the findings in Platynereis.

claim: As the brain cPRCs were recruited for vision in the vertebrate lineage, the rPRCs evolved into the retinal ganglion cells.
source: According to one hypothesis, as the brain cPRCs were recruited for vision in the vertebrate lineage, the rPRCs evolved into the retinal ganglion cells (Arendt, 2008; Arendt, 2003).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous work, supported by citations.

claim: The expression of melanopsin in intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells supports the hypothesis that rPRCs evolved into retinal ganglion cells.
source: This scenario is supported by the expression of melanopsin, an r-opsin ortholog, in the intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (Hattar et al., 2003; 2002; Koyanagi et al., 2005; Lucas et al., 2001; Panda et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on melanopsin expression.

claim: The cell-type mosaic of the vertebrate retina may have originated from the hierarchical integration of distinct cPRC and rPRC circuits mediating antagonistic behaviors.
source: we hypothesize that the cell-type mosaic of the vertebrate retina may have originated from the hierarchical integration of distinct cPRC and rPRC circuits mediating antagonistic behaviors, as observed in Platynereis larvae.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the findings in Platynereis.

claim: Each cPRC cilium branch is supported by single microtubule doublets.
source: The branches are supported by single microtubule doublets (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The total sensory membrane surface area of a Platynereis cPRC is estimated at 276 μm2 based on average diameter and total length of all branches.
source: Based on the average diameter and total length of all branches in one cPRC we estimated a membrane area of 276 μm2
evidence: This is calculated from measurements obtained from electron microscopy data.

claim: The four cholinergic cPRCs send axons to the neurosecretory plexus in the anterior nervous system.
source: The four cholinergic cPRCs send axons to the neurosecretory plexus in the anterior nervous system and synapse on four peptidergic/cholinergic RGW interneurons (labelled INRGW, and named after the expression of the RGWamide neuropeptide [Shahidi et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2017]) and four NOS interneurons (labelled INNOS, and named after the expression of the nitric oxide synthase (NOS) gene; unpublished).
evidence: This is supported by connectomics data and citations.

claim: The cPRCs synapse on a group of flask-shaped sensory-neurosecretory neurons that express diverse neuropeptides but have no postsynaptic partners.
source: The cPRCs also synapse on a group of flask-shaped sensory-neurosecretory neurons that are part of the neurosecretory anterior nervous system. These cells express diverse neuropeptides but have no postsynaptic partners (Williams et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by connectomics data and a citation.

claim: The RGW cells synapse on two serotonergic cells (Ser-h1) that are part of the ciliomotor circuitry of the larva.
source: The RGW cells synapse on two serotonergic cells (Ser-h1) that, together with their postsynaptic partner, the cholinergic MC neuron, are part of the ciliomotor circuitry of the larva (Verasztó et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by connectomics data and a citation.
